where: the danger strip on Ava's record — the chronology paragraph, the ON THE RECORD NOW / YOU TYPED pair beneath it, and the two choice buttons beneath that
finding: The two-up is fixed: matched one-line labels, both values as the figure on one baseline, provenance under each, the live cell ringed and named. It reads as one object. What it does not do is own anything, because the paragraph directly above it was rewritten in the same round to carry the identical payload in prose, and nothing came out of either. Both values and both clock times are now stated three times in three registers inside one panel — once as narrative, once as the comparison, once on the buttons. The object built to be read at a glance arrives third in the reader's path and lands as a recap of a paragraph they have already finished, so the strip has no figure: it is a block of equal-value restatements that happens to fill the entire phone fold.
evidence: The paragraph reads "You typed Chen-Ito at 9:05. At 9:08 the church office changed the same field to Ito…"; the cells then read Ito / "the church office · 9:08" and Chen-Ito / "you · 9:05"; the buttons then read "Keep Ito" and "Send Chen-Ito again". The strip runs 434→1265px on an 844px viewport, so nothing of the record below it — not the actions row, not the Profile card — is on the fold. The left cell's provenance also wraps to two lines while the right's does not, leaving a dead band in the right cell, which is the same asymmetry as last round moved one line down.
direction: Pick which register owns the comparison and let the other stop repeating it. The cells are the one built for it — labelled, aligned, ringed — so the paragraph can say what happened and who did it and leave the two values and the two times to the cells that already hold them. That also takes two or three lines off the tallest thing on the record, which is what puts the rest of the child's page back within reach.

where: the amber collision notice at the head of the sheet — the body paragraph under "Marcus Webb is editing this record too"
finding: Bold is doing two unrelated jobs in one paragraph and one of them has run away with it. Two short bold spans name the fields Marcus is changing — the fact the notice exists to deliver — and a third bold span is a 58-character instruction about where to look in the form. That third span is nearly three of the paragraph's eight lines, and it is set in the same size and weight as the notice's own heading, so the largest, brightest text mass in the block is a pointer to the interface rather than the statement of what is happening to this record. With a quarter of the paragraph emphasised, bold stops being a way to find the two field names at a glance and becomes texture; the reader has to read the whole block to recover the two words the notice is about.
evidence: Three <b> runs in one paragraph: "Last name", "Grade", and "each of those boxes says underneath what he is changing it to". Heading and body are both 14px; the heading is semibold warn, the bold spans are semibold ink-100 — brighter than the heading and, at three lines against two, physically bigger. The sibling notices already show the alternative: sync-blocked's puts its consequence line in a quiet ink-500 register under the body, and sync-outage bolds one 23-character clause and no more.
direction: Reserve the emphasis in this paragraph for the thing the paragraph is about — the fields in flight — and move the instruction about the per-field hints into the quiet register the family already has, the way sync-blocked handles its own aside. A sentence that tells the reader where to look should not out-shout the sentence that tells them what happened.

where: the quick-filter shelf under Grade / Status — "Incomplete profiles 10 · In flight 3" on line one, "Needs you 2 · Visitors 1" on line two — and the same shelf on sync-outage
finding: The counts themselves are one object again and the hue sits only in the numeral, which is right. The shelf carrying them is not composed: it wraps wherever the widths happen to run out. The two pills that state this journey's whole answer — In flight and Needs you — are adjacent in order and end up at diagonally opposite corners of the block, each sharing its line with an unrelated standing count, so the pairing the reader is meant to see is the one the wrap breaks. Both lines then stop well short of the column's right edge, which reads as spill rather than as a shelf with a deliberate ragged edge.
evidence: In a 748px column, line one ends at x=647 and line two at x=509 — 101px and 239px of empty shelf, unequal and unexplained. On sync-outage it is starker: line one holds "Incomplete profiles 10" alone, ending at x=417 with 331px empty beside it, and the alarm the page is about — "Held by the outage 10" — is pushed onto line two next to "Visitors 1". The neutral count gets a line of its own; the red one shares.
direction: Order the shelf so the pair that answers one question stays on one line and the wrap falls between groups rather than through one. Putting the job counts ahead of the standing ones would do it at these widths and would also stop the widest neutral chip claiming a line by itself on sync-outage. If a line ends short, it should be short because the group ended, not because the next chip did not fit.

where: the required markers on "First name *" and "Last name *" inside the bordered held-field group
finding: The two zones now read as two zones and a held value is plainly a value — both resolved. What survived the move into the group is the live required marker on two of the held fields, and it is the only use of the alarm accent anywhere on the sheet. Everything that speaks about the hold — the notice, the glyph, the group's one sentence — is amber, deliberately, because nothing here is wrong. So the only red marks in the frame sit on two of the fields that are merely waiting, and what they assert is a demand on the reader against controls that refuse input. Meanwhile the two fields that genuinely are hers to fill, Notes and Status, carry no marker at all, so the sheet marks as required exactly the set she cannot type into.
evidence: The asterisks sample at danger-400 — the same token as "! Failed" and "≠ Changed" on the students list. Nothing else in the sheet is in that ramp. Squint at the form and the two red ticks are the first thing that resolves, inside a group whose whole message is that nothing has failed.
direction: A held control should not wear a live requirement marker. Drop it for the duration of the hold — the group's sentence already explains why these six are not hers yet — or, if the requirement must stay visible against the moment they unlock, express it in the ink ramp so the one alarm colour on the sheet is not spent on a state that is fine.
